findings.title: Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive and can be bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive match: BlockedEmail.where(email: email). An attacker (or ordinary user) whose address is on the block list can register as "Bad@SpamClub.com" when the list contains "bad@spamclub.com" and the check will not match. The lookup should compare normalized (downcased/stripped) emails, e.g. where(email: Email.downcase(email)).

findings.title: should_block? performs writes (match_count increment) inside model validation
findings.body: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block? during User validation, and should_block? increments match_count and saves the record. In UsersController#create the user is validated via user.valid? (line 168) and then validated again by user.save, so each blocked signup attempt increments match_count twice and issues two UPDATE statements. Validations should be side-effect free; the statistics update should be moved out of the validation path (e.g. into the controller after a failed save) to avoid inflated counts, unnecessary writes, and unexpected behavior when a model is validated for other reasons.

findings.title: match_count increment is not atomic
findings.body: should_block? does record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save. Under concurrent requests two processes can read the same count and both write count+1, losing increments. Use BlockedEmail.where(email: email).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now]) or an atomic counter update.

findings.title: change_email endpoint is not covered by the blocked-email check
findings.body: The new EmailValidator (with the BlockedEmail check) only runs when email_changed? on a User record, but UsersController#change_email never assigns the new email to the user — it directly creates an email_token with the new address and sends the confirmation mail. A user can therefore sign up with an unblocked address and then switch to a blocked address via change_email, completely bypassing the blocked-email feature. The controller should also call BlockedEmail.should_block?(lower_email) (and the whitelist/blacklist check) before creating the token.

findings.title: Blocked check silently skipped when a domain-restriction error was already added
findings.body: The blocked-email check only runs if record.errors[attribute].blank?. If the email fails the whitelist/blacklist check, should_block? is never called, so match_count/last_match_at statistics for that blocked email are not recorded. This makes the analytics fields unreliable and the ordering dependency between the two checks is fragile (a future error added earlier would silently disable the block check). The block check should run independently of prior errors.
